blocks.text: Carbohydrates are naturally occurring organic compounds, including sugars, starch and cellulose and substances in bacterial cell walls and insect exoskeletons. They are major sources of energy in our diet. Chemically they are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds derived from them; the name 'hydrates of carbon' comes from formulas such as Cn(H2O)y.

Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates, the simple sugars such as glucose and fructose; they cannot be hydrolysed into simpler sugars. Their general formula is Cn(H2O)n, where n is from three to seven: a triose has three carbon atoms, a tetrose four, a pentose five and a hexose six. They are also classified by their functional group: an aldose has an aldehyde group and a ketose a ketone group. Glucose is an aldose and fructose a ketose.

Monosaccharides exist as open chains or as rings; sugars with five carbons (pentoses) or six carbons (hexoses) are more stable, and more abundant, as rings. Fructose forms a five-membered ring (furanose) and glucose a six-membered ring (pyranose). The open-chain and ring forms interconvert: the OH on C5 of glucose adds to the C=O of C1, closing the ring.

blocks.alt: Left: D-glucose as an open chain, CHO at C1, OH on the right at C2, C4 and C5 and on the left at C3, and CH2OH at C6. Middle: the six-membered ring of glucose with the ring O, CH2OH on C5 above the ring and OH groups on C1 to C4, C1 OH below (alpha form). Right: fructose as an open chain, CH2OH at C1, C=O at C2, then HO-C-H and two H-C-OH groups, and CH2OH.
blocks.caption: Open-chain and ring structures of glucose, and fructose (original diagram after Figure 27.1).
blocks.long_description: Glucose and fructose have the same formula, C6H12O6, but glucose has an aldehyde group on C1 and fructose a ketone group on C2. In water, glucose exists mainly as the ring, formed when the OH on C5 adds to the aldehyde group; only a small amount is present as the open chain.

blocks.text: The many hydroxyl groups of sugar molecules give extensive hydrogen bonding between their molecules, so pure monosaccharides are solids. In solution they form extensive hydrogen bonds with water, which makes them very soluble. Monosaccharides are an excellent source of instant energy: glucose is called blood sugar because it is present in human blood, while fructose is abundant in fruits and honey. (The thickness of honey comes from the strong hydrogen bonding of its fructose and glucose.)

Disaccharides consist of two monosaccharide units joined by a glycosidic linkage, generally with the formula C12H22O11; common ones are sucrose, lactose and maltose. They form by a condensation reaction: a hydroxyl group of one monosaccharide combines with the hydrogen of a hydroxyl group of another, releasing a molecule of water. The resulting C-O-C bond is the glycosidic bond. Sucrose, table sugar, is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose.

Polysaccharides are large molecules made of a large number of monosaccharide units joined together, with high molecular masses and the general formula (C6H10O5)n. They give monosaccharides on hydrolysis. Common examples are starch, glycogen, cellulose and pectin.

items: Starch is the main energy store of plants and consists of glucose units. It has two components: amylose, with long unbranched chains, and amylopectin, a compact, highly branched structure. Potato, sugar beet, rice and grains contain large amounts of starch.

Cellulose is the main structural material of plant cell walls. It consists of glucose units (up to about 2500) in long unbranched chains; the chains form strong hydrogen bonds with each other, making cellulose rigid and insoluble in water. In human food it is fibre, which improves gut health.
Glycogen (animal starch) is a glucose polymer stored in the liver and muscles of animals. Its structure is like amylopectin but more highly branched.

blocks.alt: Top: a hexagon labelled glucose joined through an O atom (C1-O-C2) to a pentagon labelled fructose, with the equation C6H12O6 + C6H12O6 -> C12H22O11 + H2O. Below: amylose as a straight chain of glucose hexagons (alpha-1,4 links); amylopectin as a chain with a side branch (alpha-1,6 branch point); cellulose as two straight chains linked by dashed hydrogen bonds (beta-1,4 links).
blocks.caption: Sucrose and three polysaccharides of glucose (original diagram after Figures 27.2 and 27.3).
blocks.long_description: A glycosidic link joins sugar units through an oxygen atom, with water lost. Starch and glycogen use alpha links and coil or branch into compact stores of glucose, while cellulose uses beta links that keep its chains straight, so neighbouring chains hydrogen-bond into strong fibres.
